passage:
It happened at the bus stop on an ordinary Tuesday. Nothing bad was going on. Suddenly my heart started pounding like a drum, the road tilted, and my hands went tingly. I thought I was dying. I grabbed Papa's sleeve. "Papa, something's wrong with me." Papa didn't panic. He sat me on the bench, held my hand and said, "I'm right here. It will pass. Breathe with me." He kept his voice slow. I watched his chest go up and down, and after a while mine copied it. The pounding faded. The road stayed still. Later the doctor checked me and said my heart was fine. I still don't know why it happened. But I remember Papa's calm voice.
Aadhya

qa.a: At the bus stop, on an ordinary Tuesday.

qa.q: What did Aadhya believe was happening when the road tilted?
qa.a: Aadhya was terrified and thought of dying, because the heart pounded and the hands tingled for no clear reason.

qa.q: What did Papa do that helped most?
qa.a: Papa stayed calm, sat Aadhya on the bench, held a hand and breathed slowly so Aadhya could copy him, and later a doctor checked Aadhya.

qa.q: What might Papa have felt when Aadhya grabbed his sleeve?
qa.a: Papa may have felt worried inside, but kept his voice slow so his calm could steady Aadhya.

grounding: A child's sudden pounding heart, dizziness and fear of dying come with no clear trigger and pass with a calm adult close by.

passage:
Sick room note, Friday. Urmila D'Souza, school nurse.
At 11:15 Nandini (Class 7) was brought in from the library by a classmate. She was gasping, both hands on her chest, saying, "My heart's going to burst. Am I going mad?" Her face was pale and her fingers trembled. Nothing upsetting had happened, she said; she had just been reading.
I kept my voice low and slow: "You're safe. I'm staying right here. This feeling is frightening, and it will pass." I didn't leave her side. We breathed together, long out-breaths. After a while her hands loosened and she asked for water.
I phoned her mother before lunch, explained what I saw and suggested a check-up with their family doctor. Nandini can come to me any time she feels it starting.

qa.q: What had Nandini been doing just before it started?
qa.a: Nandini had just been reading in the library.

qa.q: What was Nandini afraid of during the episode?
qa.a: Nandini was terrified that her heart would burst and that she was going mad.

qa.q: Which of Urmila's actions mattered most, and why?
qa.a: Urmila stayed right beside Nandini, spoke low and slow and breathed with her; that calm presence carried her until the feeling passed.

qa.q: How might Nandini's mother feel after Urmila's phone call?
qa.a: Nandini's mother would likely be worried, but reassured that Nandini was cared for and that a doctor's check-up is planned.

grounding: A preteen's sudden pounding heart and fear of going mad arrive with no trigger and ease with calm adult presence, followed by a doctor's check-up.
